items.title: 61531_Juan Tizol oral history interview
items.q: Oh no, I don't know anything about that.

ctx.x: Oh no, I don't know anything about that.

One of the things I wanted to get your story on was the story, that Charles Mingus tells in his book, his book, Beneath the Underdog when he says he was asked to leave Duke's band because of an incident with a trombone player and an arranger named Juan Tizol. It says, "Tizol wants you to play a solo he has written where bowing is required. You raised the solo an octave so that the bass isn't too muddy. He doesn't like that, and he comes in to the room, under the stage where you're practicing at intermission, and…

his ass upstairs. You leave the rehearsal room, proceed toward the stage with your bass, and take your place, and at the moment brings down the baton for A Train and the curtain of the Apollo Theatre goes up, a yelling, whooping Tizol rushes out and lunges at you and lunges at you with a bolo knife. The rest you remember mostly from Duke's own words in his dressing room as he changes after the show.

items.title: 61531_Juan Tizol oral history interview
items.q: The interviewee (Juan Tizol) does not speak in the provided context; the mention of Charlie Mingus is made solely by the Interviewer.

ctx.x: Juan just doesn't use that word.

But Charlie Mingus does. He's done that a lot of times, with people that work with him, and work for him, he's done the same thing, so ... Any time Mingus tells a story, I think it's good to get somebody else's version.
Right. In other words, he's prejudiced.

items.title: 67802_Charles Mingus oral history interview
items.q: There's only a few times we met. He'd always throw a couple of words my way.

ctx.x: Yeah, I went backstage, (inaudible) "I can blow better than you. Why did you give me a solo?" Pulled a knife. Of course, I saw the fire ax. It was lucky I heard about him cutting Cab Calloway; so I found out where the fire ax was. Because he didn't pull his knife (inaudible). (Inaudible). I had a similar experience with Juan Tizol of the Duke's band.
Wonderful story. And you had a fire ax then, as a matter of fact.
